issues.legal_issue: A municipal corporation may assess separate occupied portions of a building as distinct units for conservancy tax and water rates, whether their use is residential or non-residential, and the occupants need not be related as a family.
material_facts: A company constructed buildings with shops on the ground floor and residential accommodation above.
Different shop-keepers occupied the individual shops, each carrying on an independent business and having a separate source of income.
The shops had facilities connected to the municipal drainage and water systems, and the corporation assessed the shop-keepers separately.
The High Court held that the assessment rule applied only to residential buildings.
issues.conclusion: The assessment rule applied to residential and non-residential uses. A part of a building occupied as an independent unit could be treated as a separate building for assessment, and the term “family” did not require a relationship by blood or marriage.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 5(7) of the City of Nagpur Corporation Act, 1948, “building” includes a part of a building. Section 114 authorises conservancy tax and water rates, and rule 10(a), read with rules 10(b) and 10(c) of the assessment rules continued under section 3(2), permits separate assessment of qualifying portions occupied as independent units. In context, “family” can mean a person or group of persons, and “occupying” is not confined to residential use. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this interpretation.

rule.if: municipal_service_rate_assessment and separate_tenement_occupancy and occupants_have_distinct_income_sources and service_tax_conditions_met

predicates.municipal_service_rate_assessment: A municipal corporation assesses a conservancy tax or water rate on premises.
predicates.separate_tenement_occupancy: Different persons or groups occupy distinct portions of a larger building as separate units.
predicates.occupants_have_distinct_income_sources: The separate occupants have distinct sources of income.
predicates.service_tax_conditions_met: The premises meet the conditions that make them subject to the relevant municipal service tax.
predicates.each_qualifying_tenement_may_be_assessed: Each qualifying occupied portion may be assessed as a separate unit.

issues.definition: When a municipal corporation assesses a service-related rate on qualifying premises divided into distinct occupied units with occupants having separate income sources, each unit may be assessed separately.

issues.legal_issue: An occupant, rather than only the owner, may be liable for conservancy tax and water rates on occupied premises.
material_facts: The corporation issued assessment notices to individual shop-keepers who occupied separate shops.
The company had described the shop-keepers as owners in correspondence, and they were to become full owners after completing agreed payments.
The arrangement governing the shop-keepers’ occupation was not produced, and the record did not establish that they could not let the premises.
issues.conclusion: The rules did not restrict liability to owners; an occupier could be assessed. The shop-keepers also had a substantial interest in the premises and could be regarded as owners for municipal taxation if entitled to let them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 114 of the City of Nagpur Corporation Act, 1948, permits a conservancy tax payable by an occupier or owner. Section 165 contemplates that an occupier who is not the owner may be liable for tax, subject to its limitation on recovery of arrears. Rule 4 of the assessment rules requires the assessment list to state the names of persons liable. Under section 5(37), an owner includes a person entitled to receive rent; the Court observed that an occupier able to let the premises could fall within that definition.

predicates.municipal_tax_assessment: A municipal authority assesses a tax on land or a building.
predicates.person_occupies_premises: The person assessed occupies the premises in respect of which the tax is imposed.
predicates.assessment_rules_allow_occupier_liabilit: The applicable assessment framework permits an occupier to be made liable for the tax.
predicates.occupier_may_be_assessed_for_tax: The occupier may be assessed for the tax.

issues.definition: When a person occupies premises subject to municipal tax and the applicable assessment framework permits occupier liability, the occupier may be assessed.

issues.legal_issue: A delay-based challenge does not by itself require reversal of a High Court’s discretionary decision to entertain a writ petition.
material_facts: A company and a shop-keeper filed a writ petition nearly two years after later administrative proceedings concerning the assessments.

The High Court considered the procedural history, including conflicting indications about the proper remedy and further steps taken before the petition was filed, and chose to entertain it despite the delay.
The Supreme Court considered the corporation’s challenge to that exercise of discretion.
issues.conclusion: Although the delay was substantial and the High Court’s reasons might be inadequate, the Supreme Court would not set aside the High Court’s discretionary decision on delay alone.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the decision whether to entertain the writ petition despite delay as a matter of the High Court’s discretion and declined to interfere with that exercise on delay alone. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.appeal_challenges_discretionary_writ_rel: An appeal challenges a High Court’s discretionary decision to entertain a writ petition.
predicates.high_court_entertained_delayed_petition: The High Court entertained a petition despite delay in filing it.
predicates.procedural_history_provided_a_basis_for_: The High Court considered procedural events that could explain or mitigate the delay.
predicates.writ_relief_is_not_set_aside_for_delay_a: The discretionary writ relief is not reversed solely because the petition was delayed.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges discretionary writ relief granted despite delay and the procedural history furnished a basis for entertaining the petition, delay alone does not require reversal.
